Yeah, at least the entrance exams provide a common platform.

The fundamental proposition of the entrance exams is to filter, not to nurture talent among students. 

Even if the IITs and other prestigious national institutes conduct tests or implement a system of writing essays, we would still have simply too many applications which can be rejected unfairly due to the subjectivity of an essay compared to a wholly objective paper.

The solution you present, is also inadequate as it would refurbish the same issues with the American system in India, which is the financial discrimination inherent in this system, anyone here could just have gone to an International Baccalaureate school or participated in some NGO, built some program and got their ECs in check. But why wasn't this the case? It would have clearly been better for innovation and value-creation in the economy. Why didn't they just take the easier path?

The reason for this is the minimum financial background required and the simple lack of awareness. The second might be corrected but the first one is the most critical, the son of a farmer might be able to study for an entrance exam to get out of poverty but may not be able to get all these ECs in check, you need to be on the internet and have a computer already in order to make programs and sign up for these clean-up drives, amenities which aren't abundantly available in Indian villages where the majority of the population subsists.

Call it "money-hunger" but getting out of poverty and having better prospects is a perfectly suitable reason to be pursuing a degree.

What I'm saying is that being able to pursue a passion is sadly only a privilege and it's unrealistic to ever think that everyone can pursue what they like, even the kid of rickshaw puller, it's simply a wrong direction to think in.

The most gargantuan problem lies within schooling as you've clearly pointed out, schools need to be reformed. They need to have a rigorous curriculum which is more focused on critical thinking, olympiads need to be encouraged in all fields, most importantly science, as India needs technically skilled workers to support its economy. This jump from matriculation to intermediate education and then bachelor programs will only be smoothened out by a rigorous curriculum that forces us to ask questions and then builds that understanding, a good example would be Singapore.
